units.title: Major Types of World Climates
units.intro:
Climate is the long-run mix of temperature and rainfall (plus wind, humidity). Weather is today’s sample. Classification in this book is mainly by heat and rain. Vegetation is the living stamp of that pair.

**Why climates sit where they sit:** latitude (sun angle), ITCZ and pressure belts, continent vs sea, ocean currents, altitude, rain-shadow mountains. Eritrea’s plateau is cooler than its latitude because of height — always say both.

cards.title: 1.1 Introduction to Climate
body: **Climate** is the average condition of temperature and precipitation of a place over a long period of time.
The word climate comes from the Greek klima, which means the inclination of the sun.
Climate is influenced by solar radiation and by the composition of the atmosphere.
Humans, in turn, can affect climate through changing the earth’s surface and releasing pollutants such as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
The goal of the geographical study of climate is to understand its distribution over the earth’s surface.

cards.title: Step by step: Introduction to climate
body: **Step 1:** Climate is the average condition of temperature and precipitation of a place over a long period (about 30 years or more); the word comes from the Greek "klima" (slope, inclination of the Sun).
**Step 2:** Its elements are what we measure: temperature, precipitation, humidity, air pressure, wind and cloud.
**Step 3:** Its controls (factors) explain why climates differ: latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, relief and prevailing winds.
**Step 4:** Climatologists group places with similar averages into climate regions (e.g. Köppen's tropical, dry, temperate, cold and polar groups).
**Step 5:** Climate affects farming, settlement, clothing, housing and health, so it is a key link between physical and human geography.
**Example:** Asmara and Massawa have almost the same latitude, but Asmara (≈2350 m) is cool and Massawa (sea level) is hot – altitude, a control, changes the elements temperature and rainfall.

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Elements are measured, factors are reasons"
body: E-M, F-R.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Never list latitude or altitude as an "element" of climate: they are factors (controls). Elements are temperature, rainfall, humidity, pressure, wind.

cards.title: 1.2 Types of climate: the big picture
body: **Step 1: What do we sort climates by?** Climate is the average temperature and precipitation of a place over a long time, so climates are classified mainly by **temperature** and **precipitation** (rainfall).

**Step 2: Why does vegetation matter?** Every type of climate has its own **natural vegetation**, because plants grow according to the rainfall and temperature they get. If you know the climate you can predict the plants, and the other way round.
**Step 3: The five major types.** The climates of the world are divided into five major types: **Tropical**, **Dry**, **Cool**, **Cold** and **Polar**. Each one is split into smaller sub-types.

**Step 4: How to describe any climate in an exam.** Always give four things in this order: (1) **location** (latitudes and places), (2) **temperature**, (3) **rainfall**, (4) **natural vegetation**. The table below follows the same order.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Tropical climate, step by step
body: **Step 1: Where?** The Tropical climate covers almost all the land within **20° of the equator** in both hemispheres.
**Step 2: Why is it hot?** The sun is **high in the sky every day** of the year, so temperatures are high all year. This climate is controlled by **latitude** more than by any other factor.

**Step 3: Why is it wet?** The air mass is **warm, moist and unstable** (it rises easily and forms rain clouds), and the **Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)**, a belt of rising air and rain, sits over the region for much of the year.
**Step 4: Three divisions.** Tropical Wet, Tropical Monsoon and Tropical Savannah. They differ mainly in **how much rain** falls and **whether there is a dry season**.
**Africa examples:** the Congo Basin and the western coast of West Africa have the Tropical Wet climate; the savannah is widespread in Africa and reaches about 20° north and south.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Dry climates, step by step
body: **Step 1: How big?** Dry climates cover about **30% of the earth’s land**, more than any other climate group.

**Step 2: Where?** Mostly in the **sub-tropical latitudes** on the **western and central** parts of continents. In the middle latitudes (for example **Central Asia**) they occur in places **far from sources of moisture**.
**Step 3: Four types.** Sub-tropical desert, sub-tropical steppe, mid-latitude desert and mid-latitude steppe. The first two are explained below.

**Step 4: Sub-tropical desert climate.** Except for the Sahara, these deserts lie on the western side of continents. The largest are in North Africa and South-West Asia. The **Atacama** (South America) is dry because it is in the **rain shadow** of the Andes.
**Step 5: Rain.** Rainfall is **low and unreliable**; most showers are short; some deserts have gone 3 or 4 years without a drop of rain.
**Step 6: Temperature.** Summers are long and hot, with monthly averages of about **35 °C**; winter averages are **17–19 °C**; the **daily range** is very large (hot days, cold nights).
**Step 7: Vegetation.** Drought-resistant **scrub**. Plants survive by growing **long roots** deep into the ground and by **storing water** in their leaves or stems.

**Step 8: Sub-tropical steppe.** It surrounds the desert. Rain is greater and more reliable and temperatures slightly milder; the rain is seasonal, falling in summer on the equator side of the desert.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Cool climates, step by step
body: **Step 1: The idea.** Cool climates are a **transition** between the warm tropical climates and the severe mid-latitude climates. They have the **greatest day-to-day weather changes**.
**Step 2: Seasons.** The difference between the seasons is bigger for **temperature** than for rainfall. Summers are long and usually hot; winters are short and fairly mild.
**Step 3: Frost.** Unlike hot climates, cool climates get **winter frosts**, so crops cannot grow all year round.
**Step 4: Three types** (based on rainfall): **Mediterranean**, **Humid Sub-tropical** and **Marine West Coast**. Compare the first two in the table.
**Africa example:** the Mediterranean climate is found on the north coast of Africa and at the southern tip of Africa.

cards.title: 1.2.4 Cold climates, step by step
body: **Step 1: Where?** Only in the **northern hemisphere**, between **40° and 70°N**, across North America, Europe and Asia. (In the southern hemisphere these latitudes are almost all ocean, so there is no large land mass to get this climate.)
**Step 2: Temperature.** A very **wide annual range**: winters are long and cold with snow lying for weeks or months; summers are short and cool.
**Step 3: Rain.** Rain falls in most months and snow in winter; **summer** is the time of **maximum rainfall**.

**Step 4: Vegetation.** **Coniferous forest**, mostly evergreen. From Norway across northern Europe and Siberia to the Pacific it is called the **taiga**; in North America it stretches from Alaska to Canada. Its northern limit is 50°–60°N. Drier areas have grassland: **steppes** in Asia and **prairies** in North America.

**Step 5: West Margin climate.** Coast of Alaska and coastal Scandinavia: summers short and cool (about 12 °C), winters below 0 °C for at least four months, about 750 mm of precipitation spread over the year.

**Step 6: Mountain climate.** Found in the mountains of East Africa, the **Eritrean Highland**, the Ethiopian Highlands, central Asia, the Alps, the Andes and the Rockies. Pressure and temperature **fall with altitude** while precipitation **rises**. **Altitude**, not latitude, is the main control, which is why Kilimanjaro near the equator has snow.
**Eritrea example:** Asmara (2321 m) and Massawa (8 m) are at almost the same latitude, but Asmara’s mean annual temperature is about 16 °C and Massawa’s about 29 °C. The difference is altitude.

cards.title: 1.2.5 Polar climates, step by step
body: **Step 1: Why so cold?** Polar climates are **farthest from the equator**, so they get too little sunlight. **No month averages more than 10 °C**, and they have the lowest annual temperatures in the world.
**Step 2: Why so dry?** Cold air holds little moisture, and there is almost no evaporation. They are among the driest places on earth.
**Step 3: Two types** (by summer temperature): **Tundra** and **Ice Cap**.

cards.title: Why climates differ: the causes behind the table
body: **Latitude:** near the equator the sun is high every day, so the Tropical climates are hot all year. Towards the poles the sun is low, so the Polar climates never warm above 10 °C.

**Pressure and wind belts:** the rising air of the ITCZ brings rain to the tropics; sinking air of the sub-tropical high pressure brings the clear skies of deserts and of the savannah dry season. Seasonal wind reversal makes the monsoon.
**Distance from the sea and relief:** places far from moisture (Central Asia) or behind mountains (Atacama, in the rain shadow of the Andes) are dry.
**Altitude:** temperature falls with height (about 6.5 °C for every 1000 m, Grade 9), so highlands such as the Eritrean Highland are much cooler than the coast at the same latitude.
Humans can also change climate, by changing the earth’s surface and releasing gases such as carbon dioxide.

cards.title: How to write a full climate answer
body: **1. Name it:** give the climate type and sub-type (e.g. Tropical Savannah).
**2. Locate it:** latitudes plus one or two places (e.g. 5°–15°, widespread in Africa).
**3. Temperature:** give a number (e.g. 27 °C, range not more than 3 °C).
**4. Rainfall:** amount and season (e.g. 900–1800 mm, wet summer and dry winter).
**5. Reason:** say why (latitude, ITCZ, pressure belt, distance from the sea, altitude).
**6. Vegetation:** name it and one feature (e.g. tall grasses with scattered trees).
For Eritrea, stack the reasons: tropical latitude + Red Sea to the east + the height of the plateau. One-reason answers are too thin.

cards.title: Common mistakes
body: **Cool is not Cold.** Cool climates (Mediterranean, Humid Sub-tropical) have long hot summers; Cold climates have long freezing winters.
**Mediterranean rain falls in winter**, not summer. Summers are dry and sunny.
**Cold climates are only in the northern hemisphere** (40°–70°N).
**Mountain climate is controlled by altitude**, not latitude.
**The tundra lies on the Arctic Ocean coasts**, not the Antarctic Ocean; most of Antarctica is Ice Cap.
**The savannah has the least rain of the three tropical climates** (900–1800 mm) and a clear dry season.

cards.title: Tropical climates: true or false
cards.problem: True or False: (1) Tropical climate is influenced more by altitude than by latitude. (2) The air mass of the hot climate is warm, moist and unstable. (3) The largest part of the Tropical Wet climate is found in the Congo Basin of Africa. (4) The Tropical Monsoon climate covers less area than the Tropical Wet climate. (5) The Tropical Savannah climate has clear-cut seasonal changes of wet and dry seasons.

steps.text: **Method:** for each statement find the key word and compare it with the notes above.
(1) The tropical climate is influenced more by **latitude** than by any other factor. The statement says altitude, so it is **False**.
(2) The air mass is described as warm, moist and unstable. **True**.
(3) The largest areas are the upper **Amazon** Basin, the coast of West Africa, the Congo Basin and South-East Asia. The Congo Basin is only one of them, so the statement is **False**.
(4) The Monsoon climate "occupies lesser land area than the Tropical Wet climate". **True**.
(5) The unique characteristic of the savannah is a clear-cut alternation of wet and dry periods. **True**.

body: **Tip:** In True/False questions one changed word (latitude/altitude, more/less) makes the statement false. Underline it.
**Similar question:** True or False: The Tropical Wet climate has the largest annual range of temperature of all climates.
**Answer:** False. It has the smallest annual range (not more than 3 °C).

cards.title: Match the deserts
cards.problem: Match the deserts with their location. 1 Namib, 2 Thar, 3 Colorado, 4 Atacama, 5 Great Australian — A South America, B Australia, C South Africa, D Northeast India, E North America.

steps.text: **Method:** start with the easy ones whose names contain the continent, then use the list of deserts.
5 Great Australian desert is in **Australia**: 5 → B.
4 Atacama lies on the western side of **South America**, in the rain shadow of the Andes: 4 → A.
3 Colorado is one of the deserts of Central and **North America** (with Mohave and Mexican): 3 → E.
2 Thar is in **India**, and D is the only Indian option: 2 → D.
1 Namib is one of the African deserts (with the Sahara and Kalahari), on the coast of **southern Africa**: 1 → C.

body: **Tip:** Do the matches you are sure of first; the last one is then forced.
**Similar question:** In which continent are the Sahara and the Kalahari deserts?
**Answer:** Africa: the Sahara in North Africa and the Kalahari in southern Africa.

cards.title: Cool climates: true or false
cards.problem: True or False: (1) In cool climates the seasonal differences of temperature are more significant than those of rainfall. (2) In summer the Mediterranean climate has clear skies and abundant sunshine. (3) The Mediterranean climate is restricted to the northern hemisphere. (4) The Humid Sub-tropical climate covers more land than the Mediterranean climate. (5) Frost occurs more in the Humid Sub-tropical climate than in the Mediterranean climate.

steps.text: **Method:** check each statement against the cool-climate notes and the comparison table.
(1) Temperature changes between the seasons are bigger than rainfall changes. **True**.
(2) "Clear skies and abundant sunshine especially in summer" is one of its three characteristics. **True**.
(3) The Mediterranean climate is also found in central Chile, the southern tip of Africa and south-west Australia, which are in the southern hemisphere. **False**.
(4) The Humid Sub-tropical climate "is more extensive than the Mediterranean climate". **True**.
(5) Its minimum temperature is lower, so frosts occur much more frequently. **True**.

body: **Tip:** Words like "only" or "restricted" are often the trap. Look for one counter-example.
**Similar question:** True or False: Rainfall in the Mediterranean climate is concentrated in summer.
**Answer:** False. It is concentrated in winter; summers are almost without rain.

cards.title: Cold climates: true or false
cards.problem: True or False: (1) Cold climates occur only in the northern hemisphere. (2) Temperatures in cold climates stay more or less the same all year. (3) Winter is the time of maximum precipitation in these climates. (4) In the West Margin climate summers are short and cool, while winters are short and cold. (5) The major control of the mountain climate is latitude.

steps.text: **Method:** compare each statement with the cold-climate notes.
(1) Cold climates occur only in the northern hemisphere between 40° and 70°. **True**.
(2) The annual range of temperature is very wide. **False**.
(3) Summer is the time of maximum rainfall. **False**.
(4) West Margin winters are **long**, with temperatures below 0 °C for at least four months. **False**.
(5) Altitude is the major climatic control; latitude is less important. **False**.

body: **Tip:** Four "False" answers in a row is possible. Judge each statement on its own.
**Similar question:** True or False: The natural vegetation of cold climates is coniferous forest called taiga.
**Answer:** True.

cards.title: Polar climates: true or false
cards.problem: True or False: (1) Polar climates get very little sunlight because they are far from the equator. (2) Greenland is an ice plateau. (3) The tundra occupies mostly the coastal areas of the Antarctic Ocean. (4) Most of Antarctica is permanently covered with ice and snow. (5) In the Ice Cap climate all months have an average temperature below freezing.

steps.text: **Method:** compare each statement with the polar notes and the Tundra vs Ice Cap table.
(1) They do not receive adequate sunlight because they are the farthest from the equator. **True**.
(2) Both Antarctica and Greenland are ice plateaus. **True**.
(3) The tundra occupies the coastal areas of the **Arctic** Ocean. **False**.
(4) The Ice Cap climate covers most of Antarctica, where land is permanently under ice and snow. **True**.
(5) All months are below freezing in the Ice Cap climate. **True**.

body: **Tip:** Arctic = north (tundra coasts); Antarctic = south (ice cap).
**Similar question:** True or False: The tundra has at most four months with average temperatures above freezing.
**Answer:** True.

cards.title: Review I: choose the best answer, fully worked
cards.problem: (1) In studying the climate of a place we should consider: A altitude, B latitude, C topography, D distance from the sea, E all of the above. (2) The Tropical Wet climate is located between: A 0° and 5°, B 5° and 10°, C 10° and 15°, D 15° and 20° N and S. (3) A climate with scrub vegetation is: A hot, B dry, C cool, D cold, E polar. (4) Polar climates are known for: A grass, B equatorial forest, C permanently warm, D permanently hot, E permanently cold conditions. (5) The climate where land is always covered by ice and snow is: A Humid Sub-tropical, B West Margin, C Ice Cap, D Mediterranean, E Tundra.

steps.text: (1) Altitude, latitude, relief and distance from the sea all change temperature and rainfall, so **E (all of the above)**.
(2) The Tropical Wet climate extends from 0° to 5° on both sides of the equator: **A**.
(3) Sub-tropical deserts have drought-resistant scrub: **B (dry climate)**.
(4) Polar climates are known for permanently cold conditions: **E**.
(5) "Ice cap is a climate where the land is permanently covered with ice and snow": **C**.

body: **Tip:** When every option is a real factor, "all of the above" is usually right.
**Similar question:** Which climate has natural vegetation called selvas? A Savannah, B Tropical Wet, C Mediterranean, D Tundra.
**Answer:** B. The Tropical Wet climate has the tropical rainforest, also called selvas.

cards.title: Review II: fill in the blanks, fully worked
cards.problem: (1) The average condition of temperature and rainfall is called ____. (2) The difference between the highest and the lowest temperature of the day is called ____. (3) The two sub-divisions of the polar climates are ____ and ____. (4) A climate with clear skies and abundant sunshine, especially in summer, is ____. (5) The vegetation mainly found in the cold climate is ____.

steps.text: (1) Average temperature and rainfall over a long time = **climate**.
(2) Highest minus lowest temperature of one day = **daily range of temperature** (for a year it is the annual range).
(3) Polar climates are divided by summer temperature into **tundra** and **ice cap**.
(4) Clear summer skies and sunshine are a characteristic of the **Mediterranean climate**.
(5) Cold climates have **coniferous forest (taiga)**.

cards.answer: climate; daily range of temperature; tundra and ice cap; Mediterranean climate; coniferous forest (taiga)
body: **Tip:** Daily range = one day; annual range = warmest month minus coldest month.
**Similar question:** Fill in: The type of vegetation of the Tropical Savannah climate is mainly ____.
**Answer:** Tall grasses (with scattered shrubs and trees).

cards.title: Review III.1: luxuriant tropical vegetation
cards.problem: Why do we find luxuriantly growing vegetation in the Tropical Wet climate?

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the climate.** About 27 °C every month and 1500–2500 mm of rain, with rain in every month.
**Step 2: Link to plant needs.** Plants need warmth and water. Here both are available all year, so there is no cold or dry season to stop growth.
**Step 3: Write it.** High rainfall and high temperature throughout the year give excellent conditions for growth, so a dense, three-layered evergreen rainforest (selvas) grows.

cards.answer: Because high rainfall and high temperature all year give excellent conditions for plant growth.
body: **Tip:** Always connect a vegetation answer to both temperature and rainfall.
**Similar question:** Why do trees in the monsoon forest shed their leaves?
**Answer:** Because the monsoon climate has a dry season (winter winds blow from land to sea and bring no rain), so most trees are deciduous.

cards.title: Review III.2: the savannah’s unique feature
cards.problem: What is the unique characteristic of the climate of the Tropical Savannah?

steps.text: **Step 1: Name the feature.** A clear-cut seasonal alternation of **wet and dry** periods.
**Step 2: Explain the dry season.** In winter the sub-tropical high pressure dominates and gives clear skies, so it is dry.
**Step 3: Explain the wet season.** In summer the ITCZ shifts with the sun and brings wet tropical weather.
**Step 4: Add a number.** Annual rainfall is 900–1800 mm, less than in the other two tropical climates.

cards.answer: A clear-cut alternation of a wet season (summer, ITCZ) and a dry season (winter, sub-tropical high pressure).
body: **Tip:** A "why" answer should name the pressure belt or wind that causes each season.
**Similar question:** What is the main characteristic of the Tropical Monsoon climate?
**Answer:** A seasonal reversal of winds: wet summer monsoon from the Indian Ocean, dry winter winds from land to sea.

cards.title: Review III.3: three features of the Mediterranean climate
cards.problem: Explain the three major characteristics of the Mediterranean climate.

steps.text: **Step 1: Rainfall.** Annual rainfall is concentrated entirely in **winter**; summers are almost without rain.
**Step 2: Temperature.** Winters are unusually **mild**; summers vary from hot to warm.
**Step 3: Sunshine.** There are **clear skies and abundant sunshine**, especially in summer.
**Step 4: Add location for full marks.** 30°–45° N and S, mostly coastal, around the Mediterranean Sea and on the north coast of Africa.

cards.answer: Winter rain and dry summers; mild winters and hot to warm summers; clear skies and abundant sunshine in summer.
body: **Tip:** Use the three headings rain, temperature, sunshine so you never forget one.
**Similar question:** Why do tourists like to visit Mediterranean lands in summer?
**Answer:** Because summers there are dry with clear skies and abundant sunshine.

cards.title: Review III.4: cold climates only in the north
cards.problem: Explain why cold climates are found only in the northern hemisphere.

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the latitudes.** Cold climates occur between 40° and 70° latitude.
**Step 2: Look at a world map.** In the northern hemisphere these latitudes cross the huge land masses of North America, Europe and Asia.

**Step 3: Compare with the south.** Between 40° and 70°S there is almost only ocean (just the narrow southern part of South America and small islands such as New Zealand), and the sea keeps temperatures milder.
**Step 4: Conclude.** With no large land mass there, the southern hemisphere has no cold climate region.

cards.answer: Because only the northern hemisphere has large land masses between 40° and 70°; in the south these latitudes are mostly ocean.
body: **Tip:** For "why only here" questions, check where land and sea are on the map.
**Similar question:** Where is the taiga found?
**Answer:** In Europe and Asia from Norway across northern Europe and Siberia to the Pacific coast (and from Alaska to Canada in North America).

cards.title: Review III.5: dry tundra
cards.problem: Why is the availability of moisture very limited in the Tundra climate?

steps.text: **Step 1: Temperature.** The warmest month is only 4–10 °C and most months are below freezing.
**Step 2: Link to moisture.** Cold air cannot hold much water vapour, and there is almost no evaporation.
**Step 3: Result.** Annual precipitation is usually less than 250 mm, falling mostly in the warm season.

cards.answer: Because the air is too cold to hold much moisture, so annual precipitation is under 250 mm.
body: **Tip:** Cold air = little water vapour = little rain or snow.
**Similar question:** Why is there no vegetation in the Ice Cap climate?
**Answer:** Because the land is permanently covered with ice and snow and all months are below freezing.

cards.title: Identify the climate from data (1)
cards.problem: A place has an average temperature close to 27 °C in every month, an annual range of 2 °C and 2000 mm of rain spread over all months. Name its climate and its vegetation.

steps.text: **Step 1: Temperature.** Hot every month, so it is a Tropical climate.
**Step 2: Range.** A range of 2 °C is not more than 3 °C, the mark of the Tropical Wet climate.
**Step 3: Rainfall.** 2000 mm is inside 1500–2500 mm, with rain in every month: Tropical Wet again.
**Step 4: Vegetation.** Tropical rainforest (selvas).

body: **Tip:** Check three clues (temperature, range, rainfall). If all three agree you can be sure.
**Similar question:** A place has 1200 mm of rain, a wet summer and a dry winter with clear skies, at 10°N in Africa. Name the climate.
**Answer:** Tropical Savannah (900–1800 mm, wet summer with the ITCZ, dry winter).

cards.title: Annual range of temperature
cards.problem: A town’s hottest month averages 32 °C and its coolest month 25 °C. Find the annual range of temperature. Is the town more likely Tropical Wet or Tropical Monsoon?

steps.text: **Step 1: Formula.** Annual range = hottest month − coolest month.
**Step 2: Calculate.** 32 °C − 25 °C = **7 °C**.
**Step 3: Compare.** The Tropical Wet range is not more than 3 °C, so 7 °C is too large for it.
**Step 4: Decide.** The Tropical Monsoon climate runs from 25 °C in the cool season to 32 °C in the hot season, so the town is Tropical Monsoon.

body: **Tip:** Always write the subtraction; examiners give a mark for the method.
**Similar question:** An ice-cap station has a coldest month of −40 °C and a warmest month of −8 °C. Find the annual range.

cards.title: Identify the climate from data (2)
cards.problem: A coastal place at 35°S gets almost all its rain in winter. Summers are dry, sunny and warm, and winters are mild. Name the climate and give one place where it is found in Africa.

steps.text: **Step 1: Latitude.** 35° is inside 30°–45° (Mediterranean) and also 20°–40° (Humid Sub-tropical), so latitude alone cannot decide.
**Step 2: Rain season.** Winter rain and dry summers is the key mark of the Mediterranean climate (the Humid Sub-tropical has abundant rain).
**Step 3: Sunshine and temperature.** Sunny summers and mild winters agree.
**Step 4: Africa.** 35°S in Africa is the southern tip of Africa.

cards.answer: Mediterranean climate; the southern tip of Africa (also the north coast of Africa)
body: **Tip:** When latitude fits two climates, use the rain season to decide.
**Similar question:** A place on the eastern side of a continent at 30°N gets 1400 mm of rain and summer months of about 26 °C. Name the climate.
**Answer:** Humid Sub-tropical climate.

cards.title: Eritrea: why Asmara is cooler than Massawa
cards.problem: Asmara is at 2321 m and Massawa at 8 m, at almost the same latitude (about 15°N). Using a fall of about 6.5 °C per 1000 m, estimate how much cooler Asmara should be, and compare with the real means (Asmara 16.1 °C, Massawa 29.3 °C).

steps.text: **Step 1: Height difference.** 2321 m − 8 m = 2313 m.
**Step 2: Change to thousands of metres.** 2313 ÷ 1000 = 2.313.
**Step 3: Estimate the cooling.** 2.313 × 6.5 °C ≈ 15 °C.
**Step 4: Real difference.** 29.3 °C − 16.1 °C = 13.2 °C.
**Step 5: Compare.** The estimate (about 15 °C) is close to the real 13.2 °C, so altitude explains most of the difference.
**Step 6: Name the climate idea.** This is the Mountain climate of the Eritrean Highland: altitude, not latitude, is the main control.

cards.answer: About 15 °C cooler by estimate; really 13.2 °C. The cause is altitude (Mountain climate).
body: **Tip:** Same latitude but different temperature? The answer is almost always altitude.
**Similar question:** Ghinda is at 962 m. Using 6.5 °C per 1000 m, about how much cooler than Massawa (8 m) should it be?
**Answer:** (962 − 8) ÷ 1000 × 6.5 ≈ 6.2 °C cooler (the real means are 24.5 °C and 29.3 °C, a difference of 4.8 °C).

cards.title: Africa: climates from the equator northwards
cards.problem: Starting in the Congo Basin and travelling north to the Mediterranean coast of Africa, list the climate types you pass through, in order.

steps.text: **Step 1: Start.** The Congo Basin (0°–5°) has the **Tropical Wet** climate with rainforest.
**Step 2: Move north.** North of the Tropical Wet belt comes the **Tropical Savannah** (5° to about 20° in Africa) with tall grass.
**Step 3: Sub-tropical latitudes.** Next is the **Sahara**, a sub-tropical desert (Dry climate) with scrub, edged by **steppe**.
**Step 4: The coast.** On the north coast of Africa (about 30°–37°N) is the **Mediterranean** climate (Cool climate).

cards.answer: Tropical Wet → Tropical Savannah → Dry (steppe and Sahara desert) → Mediterranean
body: **Tip:** Africa is almost a mirror: the same order appears going south (savannah, Kalahari and Namib deserts, Mediterranean at the southern tip).
**Similar question:** Going south from the Congo Basin to the southern tip of Africa, which desert climate do you cross?
**Answer:** The sub-tropical desert climate of the Kalahari and Namib deserts.

cards.title: Identify the climate from data (3)
cards.problem: A station has a warmest month of 6 °C, nine months below freezing and 200 mm of precipitation a year. Name the climate. Give one reason why it cannot be Ice Cap.

steps.text: **Step 1: Is it polar?** No month above 10 °C, so yes.
**Step 2: Which polar type?** The warmest month (6 °C) is between 4 and 10 °C: Tundra.
**Step 3: Months above freezing.** Three months are above freezing (at most four is allowed): Tundra.
**Step 4: Precipitation.** 200 mm is below 250 mm: Tundra.
**Step 5: Why not Ice Cap?** In the Ice Cap climate all months are below freezing, but this station has a month of 6 °C.

cards.answer: Tundra; it cannot be Ice Cap because some months are above freezing.
body: **Tip:** Polar test: warmest month above 0 °C means Tundra; all months below 0 °C means Ice Cap.
**Similar question:** A station has all months below freezing, a coldest month of −45 °C and 100 mm of precipitation. Name the climate.
**Answer:** Ice Cap climate.

cards.title: Why is the Atacama a desert?
cards.problem: Explain why the Atacama desert in South America is very dry.

steps.text: **Step 1: Location.** It lies along the western side of South America, in the sub-tropical latitudes where most hot deserts are.
**Step 2: Relief.** The **Andes** mountains stand beside it.
**Step 3: Rain shadow.** Moist winds lose their moisture on the other side of the mountains, so the air that reaches the Atacama is dry. The desert is in a **rain shadow** position.
**Step 4: Result.** Very low and unreliable rainfall and drought-resistant scrub.

cards.answer: It is in the rain shadow of the Andes, in the sub-tropical desert latitudes.
body: **Tip:** Deserts have three common causes: sub-tropical high pressure, distance from the sea, and rain shadow.
**Similar question:** Why are the deserts of Central Asia dry, even though they are in the middle latitudes?
**Answer:** Because they are far from sources of moisture (the sea).

cards.title: How desert plants survive
cards.problem: Give two ways in which plants of the sub-tropical desert are adapted to dry conditions, and explain each.

steps.text: **Step 1: Name the vegetation.** Drought-resistant scrub.
**Step 2: First adaptation.** **Long roots** that go deep into the ground reach water far below the surface.
**Step 3: Second adaptation.** **Storing water** in leaves or stems lets the plant survive long periods without rain (some deserts get no rain for 3–4 years).

cards.answer: Long, deep roots to reach underground water; storing water in leaves or stems.
body: **Tip:** An adaptation answer has two parts: the feature and how it helps.
**Similar question:** Why is there poor undergrowth in the tropical rainforest?
**Answer:** Because the leaves and branches of tall trees stop sunshine from reaching the ground.

glossary.meaning: Climate is the average condition of temperature and precipitation of a place over a long period of time.

tips.text: Climate is the average condition of temperature and precipitation of a place over a long period of time. It has profound effects on vegetation and animal life, including humans.
Humans, in turn, can affect climate by changing the earth’s surface and by releasing chemicals such as carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
The main aim of studying climate is to understand its distribution over the earth’s surface.
To understand the diversity of world climate better, the most important aspects must be selected and studied.
Temperature, precipitation and vegetation are widely used as bases for the classification of climate.

The classification of world climates is intended to be used as a useful learning tool. It helps to simplify and organize various types of climates into a system that helps us to understand the distribution and characteristics of each type.

units.title: Soils of the World
units.intro:
Soil is a living mix: weathered rock + organic matter + water + air. Factors (CLORPT style): climate, organisms, relief, parent rock, time. Profile: O / A (topsoil, humus) → B (subsoil, washed-down clays) → C (weathered parent) → rock.

Climate makes soil as much as rock does: hot wet → deep, leached, lateritic; cold → thin, slow; dry → little organic, salty in places. Vegetation both uses and builds the humus layer. Steep slopes keep soil thin (it slides away).

cards.title: 2.1 Understating Soil
body: The process of soil formation is continuous and takes a long time.
The bed rock breaks down and mixes with dead plants and animal remains very slowly.
For example, it takes three hundred years to form one centimeter of soil in tropical areas.
Soils are formed by a process of weathering, which is the disintegration of rocks into smaller particles.

cards.title: Five factors of soil formation
head: Factor
How it works
Effect on the soil
rows: Bedrock is broken down by physical weathering (heating by day, cooling at night) and chemical weathering (decay; common in hot, wet areas).

cards.title: 2.2 Formation of Soil
body: **Soil formation** is the result of five different factors.
The nature of parent material has a strong influence on the characteristics of the soil.
Parent material is disintegrated into smaller particles through the process of weathering.
The top surface of the rock is heated and expands.

cards.title: Step by step: Formation of soil
body: **Step 1:** Soil forms when parent rock is broken down by weathering (physical and chemical) into small particles.
**Step 2:** Organisms add organic matter: plants drop leaves, and worms, insects and bacteria decompose them into humus.
**Step 3:** Climate controls the speed: heat and moisture speed up weathering and decay; dry or cold places form soil slowly.
**Step 4:** Relief (slope) matters: steep slopes lose soil to erosion and have thin soils; gentle slopes and valleys collect deep soils.
**Step 5:** Time: it can take hundreds to thousands of years to form a few centimetres of mature soil with clear horizons (O, A, B, C).
**Example:** Basalt weathering on the gentle Eritrean plateau around Mendefera produces deep, dark fertile soil, while on the steep eastern escarpment slopes soil is thin because it is washed away.

cards.title: Expanded notes
body: Good farm soil has crumb structure, dark A horizon, and a mix of sand (drain), silt and clay (hold nutrients). Laterite under rainforest looks red and can bake hard if the forest is stripped. Chernozem / prairie soils are thick and dark — bread-basket soils. Desert soils may be fertile in minerals but lack water and humus.

Texture is the sand–silt–clay mix. Structure is how those grains clump. A clay soil with good crumbs can still drain; the same clay smashed and bare will pond and then bake. pH matters: too acid or too alkaline locks nutrients even if they are present. Farmers add lime or organic matter to nudge pH and structure — not only bags of fertiliser.

On Eritrean slopes the practical sequence is: keep a cover → slow the water (terrace, contour, check dam) → put organic matter back. Wind on bare dry lowlands needs the same cover logic. Soil lost this year is not a next-season crop.

Red soils are common in desert and semi-desert environments, where the colour is derived from reddish parent materials.

cards.title: Step by step: Properties of soil
body: **Step 1:** Colour: dark/black soils are rich in humus; red and yellow soils contain iron oxides; grey or white soils are often poorly drained or leached.
**Step 2:** Texture: the proportion of sand (gritty, coarse), silt (smooth) and clay (sticky, fine); a balanced mix is called loam.
**Step 3:** Structure: how particles group into crumbs, blocks, plates or columns – crumb structure lets air and water move well.
**Step 4:** Porosity and permeability: sandy soils drain fast and hold little water; clay soils hold water but drain slowly.
**Step 5:** Soil reaction (pH): acidic (below 7), neutral (7) or alkaline (above 7); most crops grow best at about pH 6–7.5.

**Example:** A farmer rubs moist soil between the fingers: it feels gritty and falls apart → sandy, low water-holding; it feels sticky and makes a ribbon → clay, poor drainage. Adding manure improves both.

cards.title: 2.6 Soil Erosion
body: **Erosion** is the process throuhg which soil is removed by water, wind or ice.
Erosion is very active in places with no vegetation cover.

cards.title: Step by step: Soil erosion
body: **Step 1:** Soil erosion is the removal of topsoil by water, wind or ice faster than new soil forms.
**Step 2:** Water erosion goes in stages: splash (raindrops), sheet (thin layer washed off), rill (small channels) and gully (deep channels).
**Step 3:** Wind erosion lifts and blows dry, loose particles in deserts and bare fields.
**Step 4:** Human causes: deforestation, overgrazing, ploughing up and down slopes, and over-cultivation remove the plant cover that protects soil.
**Step 5:** Effects: loss of fertility and crop yields, silting of dams and rivers, desertification and floods.
**Example:** In parts of the Eritrean highlands cutting trees for fuel and building left slopes bare; heavy July–August rain then formed rills and gullies and carried soil into the dams.

cards.title: 2.7 Soil Conservation
body: In many parts of the world, soil erosion has made millions of hectares of land unproductive.
Most countries have realized that soil erosion is a danger to people and measures are now being taken to reduce the effects of erosion.

cards.title: Step by step: Soil conservation
body: **Step 1:** Soil conservation means methods that protect soil from erosion and keep it fertile.
**Step 2:** Biological methods: afforestation and reforestation, planting grass strips, cover crops, crop rotation, controlled grazing and enclosures (area closures).
**Step 3:** Mechanical (physical) methods: terracing, contour ploughing, stone bunds, check dams in gullies, and micro-dams.
**Step 4:** Fertility methods: manure, compost, fallowing, mixed cropping and correct use of fertilizer.
**Step 5:** Community action and laws (e.g. bans on cutting trees, national tree-planting campaigns) make the methods last.
**Example:** Eritrea's highland terracing, hillside closures and summer student work campaigns building bunds and planting trees slow down runoff, trap soil and let vegetation recover.

units.title: Population
units.intro:
Population geography asks how many, where, how fast, and how they move. Density = people / area. Distribution is uneven: coasts, river valleys and fertile plateaus are crowded; deserts, high ice and dense forest are thin.

Change = births − deaths ± migration. High birth + falling death (better food/health) → rapid growth (many developing regions in the 20th century). Age-sex pyramid: wide base = young, growing; column = stable; top-heavy = ageing.

cards.title: 3.1 Understanding population
body: **The term population** refers to the total number of people living in a place or a country or the world as a whole.
The population of Eritrea or Africa or the world, for example, represents the population of these specific places only.
A sub branch of Human Geography called population geography studies population growth, distributions, and densities from their spatial aspects.
**The where of people** is the basic question to be answered in the study of population in geography.
The study of population is important not only for geographers but it is also vital for humans, as a whole, who live in various regions of the earth’s surface.

cards.title: 3.2 History of World Population Growth
body: The trend of population growth of the world is not constant.
Human beings have been living for at least 1 million years.
During this period of time their level of socioeconomic development has mostly been dominated by subsistence type of living conditions.
**Population growth** is the increase in population size due to excess of birth over deaths (natural increase) and migrations.
The natural increase was the most important factor of population growth at least during the initial period of human history.

cards.title: Step by step: History of world population growth
body: **Step 1:** For most of human history growth was very slow: birth and death rates were both high (hunting and gathering, then early farming).
**Step 2:** The Agricultural Revolution (about 10 000 years ago) gave more reliable food, so population rose slowly to about 250 million by 1 AD.
**Step 3:** From about 1750 the Industrial Revolution, better food supply, medicine and sanitation lowered death rates, so growth speeded up: 1 billion around 1800.
**Step 4:** In the 20th century growth exploded (population explosion): 2 billion in 1927, 3 billion in 1960, 6 billion in 1999, 8 billion in 2022.
**Step 5:** Today growth is slowing in developed countries but remains fast in many developing countries, including much of Africa.
**Example:** Doubling time: at 2 % growth per year a population doubles in about 70 ÷ 2 = 35 years; at 1 % it doubles in about 70 years ("rule of 70").

**Step 1: Understand the context.**

$$ Natural Increase = Births - Deaths $$

cards.title: 3.4 Population Growth and Structure
body: **The population growth rate** is the rate at which a population is increases or decreases in a given year due to natural increase and net migration, expressed as a percentage of the total population.
The explanation of a population in terms of its age and gender composition is known as **population structure**.
**Age and sex** are the most basic characteristics of a population.
**A population pyramid** is a graphic representation of the percentage or the actual numbers of males and females in different age groups.
In a population structure the numerical measurement of gender distribution in a population is often expressed in terms of sex ratio.

cards.title: How a population changes
body: The demographic story many countries follow: high birth and high death (slow net growth, young deaths) → death rate falls first (health, food) while births stay high (fast growth, wide pyramid) → births later fall if school, city life and women’s options change (narrower base). Migration can hide or exaggerate all of that in one region.

Eritrea’s map of people is a climate map in disguise: the plateau holds more settled farmers; pastoral lowlands hold fewer people but over a huge area; ports are dense dots on a hot strip because of trade, not because the climate is kind. When you write “uneven distribution,” name those three belts.

Urban growth is not only “more births in town.” It is rural push (land shortage, drought, few services) plus urban pull (jobs, school, clinic). Informal housing appears when the built city lags the arrivals — that is a development sentence for Unit 4.

cards.title: 3.5 Population Problems
body: Socioeconomic, political, and cultural problems that arise due to high or low population numbers or growth rates are called **population problems**.
The limited number of secondary and tertiary economic sectors leaves large numbers of the population without work.
The required labour force in these countries is small in number and also not properly trained.
Problems of Developed Countries: Developed countries also face socioeconomic and demographic problems due to their population numbers and growth rates.
More developed regions have had a longer period of aging than the less developed regions.

cards.title: Step by step: Population problems
body: **Step 1:** Rapid growth (high birth rate, falling death rate) gives a young population with many dependants under 15.
**Step 2:** Pressure on services: not enough schools, clinics, clean water and housing.
**Step 3:** Pressure on the economy: unemployment and underemployment, low income per person, food shortages.
**Step 4:** Pressure on the environment: deforestation, overgrazing, soil erosion and land fragmentation as farms are divided among children.
**Step 5:** Urban problems from rural–urban migration: overcrowding, slums, traffic and pollution.

**Example:** If a country's population grows by 3 % a year and its food production by 2 %, food per person falls each year – this gap is why fast growth can cause food shortages even when harvests improve.

body: What is migration: Migration in broad terms is defined as the movement of people across a specified boundary for the purpose of residing.
The movement involves physical distance, and there is also a change in the normal place of residence.
Types of Migration: Migration is often classified into various types on the basis of motivation, distance, and time.
The people who conduct such movement are known as immigrants when they enter into other areas by crossing international borders.
International migrants who leave their place of origins are called **emigrants**.

cards.title: Step by step: Migration
body: **Step 1:** Migration is the movement of people to live in another place, temporarily or permanently.
**Step 2:** Types: internal (within a country, e.g. rural–urban) and international (emigration out, immigration in); voluntary or forced (refugees).
**Step 3:** Push factors drive people away: drought, poverty, lack of jobs or land, conflict.
**Step 4:** Pull factors attract them: jobs, higher wages, schools, health services, safety.
**Step 5:** Effects: source areas lose young workers but receive remittances; destination areas gain labour but face overcrowding and pressure on services.

**Example:** A young farmer leaves a drought-hit village (push: crop failure) for Asmara (pull: jobs and services). The village loses labour, while the city grows and must provide more housing and water.

tips.text: The world population in the first century AD was estimated as not more than 200 million. This number was reached after 7000 years during which humans were at their lowest level of socioeconomic development.
Their subsistence economy did not allow them to increase their numbers.
Continuous wars among dominant tribal groups, and the lack of medical services could also be cited as reasons that slowed down the growth of world population.
World population, however, reached a turning point in 1750.

Since then up to the year 2000, for example, it had reached 6 billion. This is primarily due to the introduction of science and technology in various economic sectors of many nations. There is uneven population distribution in the world.
Similarly, population density also varies from place to place. This is due to various physical and socio-economic factors.
More than half of the world population, for example, lives on the continent of Asia.
Many countries and regions in the continent of Asia also have high population densities. There are also many countries and regions in the world with sparse population distributions and densities.
The growth of a population is determined by natural and socioeconomic factors.
Birth and death rates are natural factors while those related to the cultural and economic life of the people are collectively known as socioeconomic factors.

units.title: The Concept of Development
units.intro:
Development is not only GDP. It is whether people live longer, learn, work decently, and keep the environment that feeds them. Indicators: income, literacy, life expectancy, infant mortality, access to water, energy use. HDI-style thinking mixes income + health + school even if the letters HDI are later.

Simple split: more economically developed / less — but it is a line, not two boxes. Development can be uneven inside one country (capital vs periphery). Sustainable development: meet today without wrecking tomorrow’s soil, water and climate (Unit 1–2 coming back).

cards.title: 4.1.1 Causes of Underdevelopment
body: Less developed countries have been trying to improve their economic conditions and they followed various development strategies.
In some countries, income of the population has declined.
Three reasons are often given to explain underdevelopment.
The first reason is lack of sufficient natural resources.

cards.title: 4.1.2 Requirements for Development
body: **Development** is an internal process, and different countries can follow different paths to reach an advanced level.
Every underdeveloped country should identify a long-term stable path that is compatible with its specific conditions.
For development to start as an internal process, certain conditions need to be fulfilled.
Access to resources is one of the fundamental requirements for development.

cards.title: Economic growth vs economic development
head: Point
Economic growth
Economic development
rows: The income of the country increases.
Life improves for the majority of the population.
National income, income per person, output.
Literacy, life expectancy, health, clean water and other quality-of-life measures.
Can one happen without the other?
Yes: income can rise while most people stay poor if it is not shared fairly.
Needs growth that is shared fairly.
"National income improved by 7% compared to last year."
Infant deaths fall and more children go to school.

cards.title: 4.2 Economic Measures of Development
body: Different experts have developed different measures.
Non-economic indicators, also called social indicators, reflect individual or group well-being.
The proportion of population with access to safe drinking water, levels of literacy, number of medical doctors per 10,000 people, and more. are some examples of non-economic indicators.
**Per capita income** is a widely used economic measure of development.

cards.title: Tip
body: Never use only money. Pair a cash indicator with a human one (literacy or child deaths) and one environmental caution.

cards.title: How to argue “developed” on paper
body: Pick three unlike indicators: one money (GNI or GDP per person), one body (life expectancy or infant mortality), one mind (years of school or literacy). Then add one limit: inequality (averages hide a slum next to a tower) or environment (income from mining that strips a slope).

Sectors: a farm country can still be “developing” if most people are in primary work with low yield. Factories (secondary) raise output but need power and skills. Services (tertiary) dominate rich-city job lists. Skipping straight to services without food and power is a shaky ladder.

Sustainable development in this syllabus is concrete: terrace so next year’s soil exists; manage grazing so the range is not a dust patch; use woodlots so the last highland tree is not the school stove. It is Unit 2 wearing a policy hat.

units.title: The Representation of Relief on Maps
units.intro:
Maps must show height. Methods: spot heights, layer colouring, hill shading, hachures, and **contours** (the one you must master). Contour = line of equal height. Interval is printed on the map — read it before you shout “steep”.

Packed lines = steep. Wide = gentle. Closed loop, values up inward = hill. V pointing up-valley = river valley. Gradient = rise / horizontal distance (same units). Cross-section: tick contours along a line, plot heights, join. Intervisibility: can A see B? Draw the section — a ridge in the way blocks the view.

body: Travelers mostly use these types of diagrams to obtain general information about distances, shapes, directions, and sizes of features on maps.
Ancient traveler frequently used these types of diagrams while traveling from place to place.
Nowadays they are mostly used as preliminary information about relief features in the form of simple sketches.

cards.title: 5.1.2 Hachures
body: **Hachures** are the oldest methods of showing relief.
Hachures indicate the general drainage pattern from top to bottom sections of a slope.
Steep slopes, for example, are represented by heavy and closely drawn hachures.
In gentle slopes, hachures look lighter and also drawn farther apart.

cards.title: 5.1.3 Hill Shading
body: In hill shading technique, steep slopes are shaded more darkly than gentle slopes.

cards.title: 5.1.4 Form Lines
body: Form lines give approximate idea of the area between two contour lines.
Like contours, however, they show the steepness of an area by changing the distances among each other.

cards.title: 5.1.5 Contour Lines
body: **Contour lines** are the most effective, accurate, and commonest ways of representing heights and slopes of various types of land forms.
Contours are drawn smoothly on the basis of actual field survey.
Contour lines are drawn at regular intervals.
The value of contour lines is mostly written towards the ascending side of a slope.

cards.title: 5.1.6 Others

**Triangulation survey** is a survey in which the area to be surveyed is divided into triangles.
Trignometrical stations are more accurate than the spot heights.

cards.title: Worked habits for map relief
body: Before any calculation: read the scale and the contour interval out loud. Count lines × interval for rise. Measure map distance in cm, multiply by the scale to get ground metres, then rise/run. Leave the answer as a fraction (1 in 20) and as a percent if the paper likes both.

Cross-section: mark A and B, tick every contour the line crosses, transfer ticks to graph paper with a chosen vertical exaggeration (state it — tall spikes are not “real mountains” if you stretched the vertical axis). Join with a smooth line; rivers sit at the V bottoms.

Intervisibility: draw A–B as a straight line on that section. If any land rises through the line, they cannot see each other. Trees and buildings also block, but the mark scheme first wants the landform reason. Spot heights help when a peak sits between two contours.

cards.title: 5.2.1 Even Slope
body: When the rise or fall of the ground remains constant from the bottom to the top of a landform, the slope is called an **even slope**.
The contour lines, however, are spaced at an equal horizontal distance interval.
In a gentle even slope, for example, the contour lines are spaced wider apart, while in a steep slope, they are close to one another.

cards.title: 5.2.2 Concave Slope
body: The contour lines of this type of a slope are close at the upper part and widely spaced in the lower part.
Since the slope curves inwards one who stands at the top can easily see the bottom of the slope.
In other words, inter-visibility is possible between any two objects standing on the two different heights of a concave slope.

cards.title: 5.2.3 Convex Slope
body: A slope, which bulges or curves outwards, is called a **convex slope**.
In other words, intervisibility is very difficult in this kind of a slope.

cards.title: 5.2.4 Terraced Slope
body: In a terraced slope, gradient changes several times between the top and the bottom of the mountain.
Pairs of successive contour lines, which rise gently and fall steeply throughout the mountain, represent this type of a slope.

cards.title: 5.2.5 Cliff
body: **A cliff** is a high and very steep rock or mountain generally facing a sea or a lake.
On a contour map, a sea cliff is identified by very close contours, sometimes merging into one another or even cutting the sea coast.
In overhanging cliff that lies along the coast, much of the lower part has been eroded by sea waves and its upper part overhangs its lower part.
In such cases, the contours representing this kind of landform will cross and cut one another.

cards.title: 5.2.6 Escarpment
body: An escarpment (Scarp) is a comparatively long and regular steep face of a hill, ridge or a plateau.
The erosion of tilted landforms, for example, result in escarpments.
Faulting processes also create escarpments.
The formation of dips is associated with escarpments.
